title: Pachomius
hookLine: a former soldier organizes monks into communities with shared work and prayer

cards: Down the Nile goes a boatload of new recruits, kept under guard at night, more like prisoners than soldiers. One of them is a young Egyptian, just drafted into the army.
At one town, strangers come down to the boat with food and drink and look after them. He asks who these people are. Christians, he's told: kind to everyone, for the sake of God.
That night, the story of his life says, he made a promise: if he got free, he would serve God and serve people. His name is Pachomius.

teach.b: First, the kindness keeps working. Released from the army, Pachomius is baptized and goes to learn the desert life from an old hermit named Palamon. Hard teaching: little food, long prayer, manual work.
Second, the new thing. Anthony's way, three days ago, was mostly the hermit's way, alone or nearly. Pachomius gathers monks into a community.
At a deserted village called Tabennesi, the story goes, he begins to build.

teach.h: ONE WALL, ONE RULE, ONE TABLE.
teach.b: One wall around them all. One rule. One table.

The monks weave mats and baskets, farm, cook and nurse the sick, and what they make is for everyone. They pray together at set times. An abbot leads, and the brothers obey him, not as a general but as a father.
Third, why it matters. The hermit's life suits a few. A shared life can hold many: the strong and the weak, the gifted and the ordinary.
Some readers see in his communities the picture in Acts, where the believers held all things in common.
Shared work can wear off rough edges in a way solitude may not, because the brother who annoys you is at breakfast tomorrow. Catholic religious orders that live in community stand in that line.
Fourth, look back at this week. Under persecution, they hid the books. With Constantine came freedom, and its dangers.
Helena went to see. Anthony heard and went. Abba Moses said the cell teaches.
Syncletica said the desert is within. And Pachomius says what the desert needed to hear: you don't have to go alone.

how: Catholic monks and nuns who live in community share meals, work and the prayer of the hours under a rule and a superior, and the Church honors Saint Pachomius as a founder of that common life.

o: the soldier who gathered monks into one shared life
a desert monk who lived alone on top of a pillar
the hermit who first taught Anthony in the desert

s: Pachomius was a soldier before he was a monk
drafted as a young man; the kindness of Christians to the recruits turned him.
Pachomius's monks each lived alone and rarely met
they shared one wall, one rule, one table, work and prayer.
Pachomius taught himself the desert life
he first learned from an old hermit named Palamon.

games.q: you're a young recruit under guard on the Nile. strangers come with food and look after you. they're Christians. what do you do?
o: promise to serve God and people if you get free.
slip away with them that night.
games.why: his life says he made that promise, and kept it: baptism, the hermit Palamon, and then a whole community.

practice: Think through the work of your day, dishes, a report, a ride to school, a meal, and pick one task you usually do alone.
Picture doing it beside someone instead, not handing it off but side by side, the way Pachomius's monks wove and cooked together. If you pray, ask a blessing on the work you share.

wordCard.voice: Pachomius. A former soldier, won over by strangers' kindness, who gathered monks into communities of shared work and prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing — the word Acts uses for the believers' common life.

carryVoice: Your line: together in the desert. Nobody has to walk it alone. That's the week.
